records.name: Karabük
records.current_summary: Inland Black Sea province, conservative province. No province-specific trans-related findings in this research pass; the national framework and its 2025-26 escalation apply here unchanged. The region's own sources are national-level: a leaked draft omnibus reform package (11th Judicial Package, October 2025) would create new anti-LGBT articles — criminalising conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality", restricting gender-affirming healthcare with a minimum age of 25, and enabling charges against trans people and their providers; the state's "Year of the Family" institutional programme and blanket bans on LGBTI public events are national practice, not provincial choices. Per the country research dossier, the absence of a documented provincial ban here is not evidence of tolerance — the national blanket-ban practice applies across the country.

sources.claim: National-framework source (applies country-wide; no provincial breakdown): HRW news release, Oct 29, 2025, reports a leaked omnibus draft ("11th Judicial Package") that would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years' prison, participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years, and would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25 with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and trans people receiving deemed-illegal care up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft; HRW warns it would force treatment underground and expose people to arrest and pretrial detention.

National-framework monitoring report (applies country-wide; no provincial breakdown): Kaos GL's 2025 review finds hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy — "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions, an LGBTI+ association closed for the first time in years with criminal cases against 11 of its members, and artistic events cancelled or banned. The report documents 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings (trans people the most affected), 89 torture/ill-treatment violations (up from 51 the prior year), roughly 313 total violations overall — about 2.5 times the previous year — with 299 detention decisions, and freedom-of-expression violations rising from 216 to 540.

records.name: Kırıkkale
records.current_summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): central; military-industrial conservative. Scored relative to the national score (0.15) for Turkey.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch news release (29 October 2025): a leaked draft omnibus reform (the '11th Judicial Package') would amend the penal code so that acting 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' — or its promotion — carries up to three years in prison (an amendment to article 225 on 'indecent acts'), restrict gender-affirming healthcare to people 25 and over under onerous eligibility rules, and allow criminal charges against trans people and the professionals who treat them; justified as protecting 'the family' and 'public morals'. HRW called it one of the most alarming rights rollbacks of the decade and urged withdrawal.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's national 'LGBT rights in Turkey' page is the framework every Turkish province, Kırıkkale included, stands under: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the military: the armed forces' health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual' illness making members unfit for service, and conscripts who declare their homosexuality have to provide photographic proof. Same-sex marriage is not recognised; a 2012 constitutional-writing request to include it was rejected by both the AKP and the MHP. Authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years and police have used tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans; on 14 June 2019 the 7th Izmir Pride, the 3rd Antalya Pride and the 27th Istanbul Pride were banned by the cities' governors. The page also records a February 2026 newspaper report that the government was considering a law criminalising publicly encouraging 'behavior contrary to biological sex', with a sentence of one to three years in prison.

sources.title: Türkiye - Amnesty International country report (Report 2025/26)
sources.claim: Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26) is the enforcement framework a trans visitor stands under in any province, Kırıkkale included: in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained; although in November a court overturned a ban in Istanbul governorate as 'disproportionate' and 'unlawful', prosecutions involving 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an Izmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had engaged in activities outside its stated purpose and shared 'obscene' images incompatible with the law. Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 - an unprecedented assault that would criminalise any expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible - but they were ultimately not submitted to parliament.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.claim: National-framework reference that governs this region record under rule 1, since Kırklareli stands under Turkey's state law. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman Empire adopted a new penal code in 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender (after surgery) since 1988. However, Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military, and same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition (no marriage, civil union, or adoption). Authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants; in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th out of 49 assessed countries. For this record: the legal protections a trans or LGBTQ visitor has (or lacks) are set entirely by this national framework; no Kırklareli-specific deviation is documented.
